analysis.one_liner: Requires the President to sell off private businesses and investments to eliminate conflicts of interest.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the House Oversight Committee from July 2017 until the Congress ended in January 2019, with only one cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require any President, right after taking office, to sell all private businesses and investments — hotels, golf courses, casinos, and any other holdings — and put the money into conflict-free assets like Treasury bonds or diversified mutual funds. Violating the requirement would count as an impeachable offense under the Constitution. The bill was referred to the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens who want assurance that presidential decisions are not influenced by the President's own business holdings. Federal employees and businesses competing against the President's companies would also gain a level playing field.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Citizens wary of presidential conflicts of interest

how_it_helps.text: Requires the President, immediately after taking office, to convert all privately owned businesses and investments into cash, then buy Treasury securities, diversified mutual funds, or other holdings that cannot create a financial conflict of interest [S2] [S3].

Explicitly covers hotels, golf courses, resorts and spas, casinos, for-profit education systems, modeling and pageant companies, reality TV interests, and retail products — the asset types that can put a President's personal fortune in direct tension with policy decisions [S3].
Makes a violation a 'high crime and misdemeanor' under the Constitution's impeachment clause, giving the requirement legal teeth rather than relying on voluntary compliance [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: A President with a private business empire would have to sell those assets and accept the return limits of conflict-free holdings. Family members who run such businesses would lose the ability to keep them while the President serves.
analysis.who_pays_short: A President with private business holdings

drawbacks.text: The bill applies only to the President and Vice President-level office, not to other officials, and it does not address business interests held by a President's family members who are not in office — so much of the practical conflict problem could remain [S3].

Forcing a quick sale of illiquid assets like golf courses and hotels could produce distressed prices, and a President could argue this burdens a person for winning office; an honest supporter would acknowledge the divestiture requirement is unusually blunt [S3].
Making a violation an impeachable offense is a constitutional judgment Congress has generally avoided writing into statute, which is a real objection even for supporters of divestiture [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — removing the President's personal finances from decisions of state — is substantial, and the enumerated asset list shows the drafters were targeting a specific real-world conflict problem. The costs are real but narrow: the burden falls only on whoever holds the office, and the divestiture approach is blunter than a blind trust. On balance the bill aimed at a genuine conflict-of-interest problem with a proportionate, if aggressive, remedy.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never scheduled a hearing or a vote, so it died when the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Dwight Evans introduced the bill on July 28, 2017, with Jim McGovern as its sole cosponsor [S1] [S4].
The House referred it to the Committee on Oversight and Government Reform on the day of introduction, and the action history shows no hearing, markup, or floor action afterward [S5].
The 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, with the bill still in committee; a bill not passed by both chambers before a Congress ends dies and must be reintroduced from scratch [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: A President with private business holdings — hotels, golf courses, and other ventures — kept them and the conflict-of-interest status quo continued, since the committee never acted and no alternative divestiture requirement was enacted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Presidential business interests kept their holdings

for.name: Rep. Dwight Evans
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require presidential divestiture of conflicting business assets

against.name: House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral: no hearing, no markup, no vote was ever scheduled in the roughly 17 months before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: Both supporters were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored the bill; the majority-party-controlled committee never acted on it [S1] [S4] [S5].

industries.industry: Presidential family business interests (hotels, golf courses, resorts, casinos)
industries.note: The bill would have forced a sitting President to sell exactly these asset types and reinvest in conflict-free holdings. Defeat of the bill left those businesses intact and operating during the presidency.

industries.industry: Hospitality and golf resort competitors of presidential ventures
industries.note: Businesses competing with a President's hotels and golf courses claimed they were disadvantaged by that association; the bill would have removed the conflict but was defeated, leaving their competitive concern unresolved.
